questions.question: What is the image $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{C})$ of a set $\boldsymbol{C}\subseteq\boldsymbol{X}$?
options: The set of outputs $\boldsymbol{y}$ obtained as $\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})$ for some $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{C}$.
The set of all inputs in $\boldsymbol{X}$ that are not in $\boldsymbol{C}$, so that $\boldsymbol{f}$ avoids $\boldsymbol{C}$.

questions.question: What is the preimage $\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})$ of a set $\boldsymbol{V}\subseteq\boldsymbol{Y}$?
options: The set of inputs $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}$ such that $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})\in\boldsymbol{V}$.
Only the points of $\boldsymbol{V}$ that have unique inputs.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ be $f(x,y) = x+y$. What is the image of $[0,1]\times[0,1]$?
For $f(x,y) = x+y$, what is the preimage of $\{0\}$?
Let $f(x,y)=\dfrac{1}{x^2+y^4+1}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. For which $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is $f\bigl(f^{-1}(V)\bigr)\neq V$?
Let $\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $\boldsymbol{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be non-empty. Which situation can occur?
For $f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(x,y) = x$, what is the image of the disc $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2+y^2 \leq 1\}$?
For $f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(x,y) = x$, what is $f^{-1}([2,3])$?
Why may $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V}))$ be a proper subset of $\boldsymbol{V}$?
options: The set $\boldsymbol{V}$ must lie in the domain.
Some points of $\boldsymbol{V}$ may not be hit by any input of $\boldsymbol{f}$.
Images are always larger than their target sets.

questions.question: Why does the notation $\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})$ not require $\boldsymbol{f}$ to have an inverse function?
options: It is defined only for bijective $\boldsymbol{f}$, so an inverse always exists when it is used.
It denotes the outputs $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})$ for $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{V}$, so no inverse is involved.
It denotes the set of inputs mapped into $\boldsymbol{V}$, not a value of an inverse function.
It requires $\boldsymbol{f}$ only to be injective, so each point of $\boldsymbol{V}$ has exactly one preimage.

questions.question: Let $f(x,y) = x+y$ and $\boldsymbol{C} = \{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\}$. What is $f(\boldsymbol{C})$?
Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ be $f(x,y) = x$. Which point lies in $f^{-1}([2,3])$?
What kind of elements does $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{C})$ contain?
What kind of elements does $\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})$ contain?
options: Points in the codomain that are not attained by $\boldsymbol{f}$.

questions.question: Is $\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})$ necessarily a subset of the domain or the codomain?
options: A subset of both in every case.
Neither; it is always a number.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be $f(x)=x^2$. What is $f(\{-1,0,1\})$?
Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be $f(x)=x^2$. What is $f^{-1}(\{4\})$?
Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be $f(x)=x+1$. What is $f^{-1}([1,3])$?
Why does the notation $\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})$ not require an inverse function?
options: It always denotes a single inverse value.
It is defined only when $\boldsymbol{f}$ is a bijective function.
It denotes a set of inputs mapping into $\boldsymbol{V}$.
